extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; aspiring writers, critics, and public speakers in polite society
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and criteria for recognizing, judging, and cultivating a 'fine taste' in writing (and allied guidance on oratory, imagination, and moral purpose of drama/worship). Targets aspiring writers, critics, and public speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music in religious worship (purpose and effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applied to religious worship, music purifies and exalts the passions and strengthens devotion; it produces more lasting and permanent impressions than words alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musick, when thus applied, raises noble Hints in the Mind of the Hearer, and fills it with great Conceptions. It strengthens Devotion, and advances Praise into Rapture. It lengthens out every Act of Worship, and produces more lasting and permanent Impressions in the Mind, than those which accompany any transient Form of Words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama's moral origin and function
rubrics_metrics.description: The original form of drama (a chorus hymn) had a religious/moral purpose and should continue to mark vice and recommend virtue; the chorus's role is to intercede for the innocent and implore vengeance on the criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first Original of the Drama was a Religious Worship consisting only of a Chorus... the Chorus so far remembered its first Office, as to brand every thing that was vicious, and recommend every thing that was laudable, to intercede with Heaven for the Innocent, and to implore its Vengeance on the Criminal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between solitude and public life
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed life — alternating solitude and public usefulness — is preferable to extremes of solitary retirement or continual public agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most philosophers run into extremes praising entirely either Solitude or publick Life; in the former Men generally grow useless by too much Rest, and in the latter are destroyed by too much Precipitation. Those who, like you, can make themselves useful to all States, should be like gentle Streams, that not only glide through lonely Vales... but visit populous Towns in their Course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory: study and use of gesture and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper gestures and vehement exertions of the voice should be deliberately studied by public orators because they comment on and enforce the speech, keep the audience awake, and show earnestness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper Gestures and vehement Exertions of the Voice cannot be too much studied by a publick Orator. They are a kind of Comment to what he utters, and enforce every thing he says, with weak Hearers, better than the strongest Argument... They keep the Audience awake, and fix their Attention... they shew the Speaker is in earnest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory anti-patterns: avoid ridiculous gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the ridiculous or distracting gestures common among English speakers (hands in pockets, fiddling with a hat, twisting thread) — either use no gesture at all or only those that are graceful and expressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is often nothing more ridiculous than the Gestures of an English Speaker; you see some of them running their Hands into their Pockets... turning his Hat in his Hands... a Counsellor who never pleaded without a Piece of Pack-thread in his Hand... We ought either to lay aside all kinds of Gesture... or at least to make use of such only as are graceful and expressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions as principles of action; govern not extinguish
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions are the principles that move human actions and are necessary to animate the understanding; reason should govern and guide them, not extinguish them entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All Passions are in all Men... they must necessarily arise from the Passions, which are to the Mind as the Winds to a Ship... Reason must then take the Place of Pilot... we must endeavour to manage them so as to retain their Vigour, yet keep them under strict Command... we must govern them rather like free Subjects than Slaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'fine taste' in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine taste is the faculty of the mind which discerns the concealed faults and nicest perfections in writing; it delights in beauties and dislikes imperfections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: I may define it to be that Faculty of the Soul, which discerns the Beauties of an Author with Pleasure, and the Imperfections with Dislike.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to test whether you possess fine taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge your taste by reading celebrated works of antiquity and moderns admired by polite contemporaries; if you are not unusually delighted by such works, you likely lack the faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If upon the Perusal of such Writings he does not find himself delighted in an extraordinary Manner... he ought to conclude... that he himself wants the Faculty of discovering them. Read the celebrated Works of Antiquity... or those Works among the Moderns which have the Sanction of the Politer Part of our Contemporaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate specific authorial qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: A refined reader discerns the specific, distinguishing qualities of great authors (e.g., Livy's manner of telling a story, Sallust's insight into internal motives, Tacitus's display of external motives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe whether he tastes the distinguishing Perfections... whether he is particularly pleased with Livy for his Manner of telling a Story, with Sallust for his entering into those internal Principles of Action... or with Tacitus for his displaying those outward Motives of Safety and Interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to cultivate and improve fine taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate taste by frequent reading of the most polite authors, conversation with men of polite genius, and study of critics who penetrate the spirit and sources of literary pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most natural Method... is to be conversant among the Writings of the most Polite Authors. Conversation with Men of a Polite Genius is another Method... It is likewise necessary... to be well versed in the Works of the best Criticks both Ancient and Modern... critics who... enter into the very Spirit and Soul of fine Writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of national/local false tastes (epigram/forced conceits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid local fashions of taste that prize epigrams, forced conceits, and superficial wit which do not enlarge or better the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Our general Taste in England is for Epigram, Turns of Wit, and forced Conceits, which have no manner of Influence, either for the bettering or enlarging the Mind... I have endeavoured... to banish this Gothic Taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual description as the source of imaginative pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasures of the imagination arise chiefly from visible objects seen or recalled via painting, statue, or description; sight furnishes the imagination with ideas and is the most delightful sense for such pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Our Sight is the most perfect and most delightful of all our Senses... It is this Sense which furnishes the Imagination with its Ideas; by the Pleasures of the Imagination... I mean such as arise from visible Objects, either when we have them actually in our View, or when we call up their Ideas in our Minds by Paintings, Statues, Descriptions.
